title: Ἑρμῆς καὶ ἀγαλματοποιός
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 108 (= Perry 88). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἑρμῆς βουλόμενος γνῶναι ἐν τίνι τιμῇ παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἐστίν, ἧκεν ἀφομοιωθεὶς ἀνθρώπῳ εἰς ἀγαλματοποιοῦ ἐργαστήριον.
sentences.tr: Hermēs boulomenos gnōnai en tini timēi para anthrōpois estin, hēken aphomoiōtheis anthrōpōi eis agalmatopoiou ergastērion.
sentences.l: Hermes, wishing to know in what honour he stands among men, came, having been made like a man, into an image-maker's workshop.
sentences.i: Hermes, wishing to learn what standing he had among men, came in the likeness of a man to a sculptor's workshop.
sentences.n: ἐν τίνι τιμῇ … ἐστίν is an indirect question that keeps the indicative and the present tense of the direct one. ἀφομοιωθείς, aorist passive participle, is 'having been made like' and takes the dative of what one is made like; gods walk the earth disguised throughout these fables. ἄγαλμα is properly the image of a god set up for worship, whence ἀγαλματοποιός, the maker of such images.

sentences.t: Καὶ θεασάμενος Διὸς ἄγαλμα ἐπυνθάνετο πόσου.
sentences.tr: Kai theasamenos Dios agalma epynthaneto posou.
sentences.l: And having caught sight of a statue of Zeus he asked for how much.
sentences.i: And catching sight of a statue of Zeus, he asked the price of it.
sentences.n: πόσου is the genitive of price standing alone as the whole question, 'for how much?'. Greek puts price in the genitive with verbs of buying and selling, and the idiom runs through the rest of the fable.

sentences.t: Εἰπόντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ὅτι δραχμῆς, γελάσας ἠρώτα τὸ τῆς Ἥρας πόσου.
sentences.tr: Eipontos de autou hoti drachmēs, gelasas ērōta to tēs Hēras posou.
sentences.l: And he having said that it was for a drachma, laughing he asked for how much the one of Hera was.
sentences.i: And when the man said a drachma, he laughed and asked the price of the Hera.
sentences.n: Εἰπόντος … αὐτοῦ is a genitive absolute again. A drachma was about a day's wage for a skilled workman, so the father of the gods is going at the price of a day's labour. τὸ τῆς Ἥρας is 'the one of Hera' — ἄγαλμα is left out and the neuter article carries it.

sentences.t: Εἰπόντος δὲ ἔτι μείζονος, θεασάμενος καὶ αὐτοῦ ἄγαλμα ὑπέλαβεν ὅτι αὐτόν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ ἄγγελός ἐστι καὶ ἐπικερδής, περὶ πολλοῦ ποιοῦνται οἱ ἄνθρωποι.
sentences.tr: Eipontos de eti meizonos, theasamenos kai autou agalma hypelaben hoti auton, epeidē kai angelos esti kai epikerdēs, peri pollou poiountai hoi anthrōpoi.
sentences.l: And he having said 'for still more', catching sight of a statue of himself as well, he supposed that men make much of him, since he is both a messenger and a giver of gain.
sentences.i: And when the man named a higher price still, Hermes caught sight of a statue of himself too, and supposed that men set great store by him, being as he is both the messenger of the gods and the giver of profit.
sentences.n: μείζονος is once more the genitive of price, 'at more'. περὶ πολλοῦ ποιοῦνται is a fixed idiom — to make a thing a matter of much, hence to value it highly. ἐπικερδής, 'gainful', names Hermes' commercial side: he is god of the market and of profit as well as herald of the gods, and it is on that account that he expects to be dear.

sentences.t: Διόπερ ἐπυνθάνετο ὁ Ἑρμῆς πόσου, καὶ ὁ ἀγαλματογλύφος ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἐὰν τούτους ἀγοράσῃς, τοῦτόν σοι προσθήκην δώσω. »
sentences.tr: Dioper epynthaneto ho Hermēs posou, kai ho agalmatoglyphos ephē· « All’ ean toutous agorasēis, touton soi prosthēkēn dōsō. »
sentences.l: Wherefore Hermes asked for how much, and the image-carver said: « Well, if you buy these, I will give you this one as an addition. »
sentences.i: So Hermes asked what that one cost, and the carver said: « Why, if you buy those two, I will give you this one into the bargain. »
sentences.n: Chambry's text changes the craftsman's name in mid-fable — ἀγαλματοποιός at the start, ἀγαλματογλύφος here, 'image-maker' and 'image-carver' — and the literal line keeps the difference rather than levelling it. προσθήκη is what is added on to a purchase, the small thing thrown in with the sale. ἐάν with the aorist subjunctive is the ordinary vivid future condition.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα κενόδοξον ἐν οὐδεμίᾳ μοίρᾳ παρὰ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὄντα ὁ λόγος ἁρμόζει.
sentences.tr: Pros andra kenodoxon en oudemiāi moirāi para tois allois onta ho logos harmozei.
sentences.l: The story fits a vainglorious man who is in no reckoning at all among the rest.
sentences.i: The story fits a man full of his own importance who counts for nothing with anyone else.
sentences.n: κενόδοξος is 'empty-glorious', full of his own reputation and of nothing else. ἐν οὐδεμιᾷ μοίρᾳ ὄντα is idiomatic: μοῖρα is a share or a reckoning, and to be in no reckoning is to be held of no account. The closing sentence crosses the collection's two commonest shapes — πρός with the accusative naming the target, but ἁρμόζει, 'fits', where εὔκαιρος usually stands.
